hints: Focus on what the word ionisation really means, are we removing an electron or adding one?
Remember the definition always starts from one isolated gaseous atom, so think whether iodine should be written as $\text{I(g)}$ or $\tfrac{1}{2}\text{I}_2\text{(g)}$.
Put those two ideas together to pick the equation that shows one gaseous atom losing one electron to form a 1+ ion.
walkthrough:
**Recall the definition of first ionisation energy**

First ionisation energy is the energy needed to remove one electron from each atom in one mole of gaseous atoms to form one mole of gaseous 1+ ions. It is always about loss of an electron.

General equation:
$$\text{X(g)} \rightarrow \text{X}^{+}\text{(g)} + \text{e}^{-}$$

**Check the starting species**

The starting material must be single, isolated gaseous atoms, $\text{I(g)}$. Even though iodine exists as $\text{I}_2$ molecules in a bottle, the definition insists we start from $\text{I(g)}$.

So any equation starting with $\tfrac{1}{2}\text{I}_2\text{(g)}$ cannot be correct for this definition.

**Check the process**

We need removal: $\text{atom} \rightarrow \text{ion}^{+} + \text{e}^{-}$. Equations that show $+ \text{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{I}^{-}$ are adding an electron, that is electron affinity, the opposite process.

Only $\text{I(g)} \rightarrow \text{I}^{+}\text{(g)} + \text{e}^{-}$ matches both conditions.

options.A: Shows an electron being added to form $\text{I}^{-}\text{(g)}$, which is electron gain, not ionisation. It also starts from $\tfrac{1}{2}\text{I}_2\text{(g)}$ instead of $\text{I(g)}$. This is a version of electron affinity, not ionisation energy.
options.B: Starts correctly from $\text{I(g)}$ but adds an electron to make $\text{I}^{-}\text{(g)}$. That is the equation for the first electron affinity of iodine. Students who mix up gain and loss of electrons pick this.
options.C: Shows the correct process of electron loss to form $\text{I}^{+}$, but starts from the wrong species, $\tfrac{1}{2}\text{I}_2\text{(g)}$. The definition requires one mole of isolated gaseous atoms, $\text{I(g)}$. Students who think about the normal state of iodine as $\text{I}_2$ are tempted by this.
options.D: Perfectly matches the definition: one gaseous iodine atom, $\text{I(g)}$, loses one electron to form one gaseous $\text{I}^{+}\text{(g)}$ ion plus an electron. Correct state symbols, correct species, and correct direction for first ionisation energy.
